title: Enhancing lighting design through the investigation of illuminance and correlated color Temperature's effects on brain activity: An EEG-VR approach
research_question: Will brain activity features (i.e., EEG data) be modulated in a predictable fashion during the first seconds of exposure to varied illuminance levels (RQ1a) and CCT (RQ1b)? Will it be possible to associate specific EEG patterns with specific lighting conditions, in terms of illumination and CCT (RQ2)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' subjective mood responses (RQ3a: pleasure, RQ3b: arousal)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' behavioral choices of desired vs. non-desired lighting (RQ4)?

participants.description: 33 healthy adult participants recruited, 8 excluded due to technical problems. Final sample N=25 (15 female, 10 male), age 18-64 years (mean 24.4, SD 8.3). All associated with Cornell University (21 undergrads, 4 grad students/faculty). No medical eye problems, no difficulty distinguishing colors. 64% used eyeglasses/contacts. All reported 7-9h sleep prior.
participants.recruitment: convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and announcements on departmental e-mail lists)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Modern interior office room (4.0m x 7.4m x 3.0m) in Unreal Engine 4.26. Participants seated at a desk. 17 specific artificial lighting conditions tested from a matrix of 7 illumination levels (300lm to 4500lm) and 7 CCT levels (1500K to 7500K). Lighting sources were six double tube-lights on the ceiling. Presented via Meta Quest 2 HMD (1832x1920 pixels/eye, 100 nits max brightness).

measures.instrument: Electroencephalography (EEG) with 22 Ag/AgCl channels (10-20 international layout), 250 Hz sampling rate (downsampled to 100 Hz)
Igroup Presence Questionnaire (IPQ) 7-point Likert scale (overall presence, spatial presence, involvement, experienced realism)
Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) (nausea, oculomotor disturbance, disorientation)
Participant adjustment of illumination (100 lm intervals) and CCT (100 K intervals) to optimal preference

findings.consequent: EEG alpha/theta (α/θ) and beta/theta (β/θ) band-power ratios
findings.mechanism: Modulation of brain activity in parietal and central regions.
findings.quote: Regarding illuminance, our EEG analysis found a strong modulation of band-power ratios. The illumination level and the ratios of α/θ and β/θ were positively associated in both parietal and central regions of the brain

findings.consequent: EEG theta band strength
findings.mechanism: Modulation of brain activity in frontal brain regions.
findings.quote: in frontal brain regions, illuminance was negatively associated with theta band strength

findings.mechanism: Modulation of brain activity in frontal brain regions.
findings.quote: as well as negatively associated with the α/β and α/γ ratios

findings.antecedent: Lighting condition N1 (4500K CCT, 300lm) vs N6 (4500K CCT, 4500lm)
findings.consequent: Brain activity (EEG features)
findings.mechanism: Machine learning classification (quadratic kSVM) achieved 68% accuracy.
findings.quote: The results for comparing N1 vs. N6 (large illumination differences at the "neutral" 4500 K CCT level) across all EEG features yielded 68% classification accuracy.

findings.consequent: Brain activity (EEG features)
findings.mechanism: Machine learning classification (quadratic kSVM) achieved 74% accuracy.
findings.quote: For the M1 vs. M6 comparison (large CCT differences at the "medium" 2400 lm illumination level), we achieved 74% classification accuracy.

findings.antecedent: Higher beta (13-30 Hz) power compared to theta (4-7 Hz) power in parietal regions
findings.consequent: Greater illumination
findings.mechanism: Consistent EEG pattern with positive linear association.
findings.quote: The most consistent EEG pattern when evaluating illumination level conditions was that higher β power (13-30 Hz) compared to θ power (4-7 Hz) in parietal regions was found to have a positive linear association with greater illumination.

findings.consequent: Theta-band (θ) power in frontal regions
findings.mechanism: Reduction of theta-band power.
findings.quote: a reduction of theta-band (θ) power in the frontal regions associated with higher illumination

findings.antecedent: Parietal brain region activity (power relative to β and β power relative to θ)
findings.consequent: Level of illuminance in the VR space
findings.mechanism: Positive and significant correlation.
findings.quote: Parietal brain region activity including (a) a power relative to β and (b) β power relative to θ, were observed to have a positive and significant correlation with the level of illuminance in the VR space.

findings.antecedent: Broadband frontal neural synchronization (higher power) at 4-50 Hz (with smaller effect at β-band 13-30 Hz)
findings.consequent: Color temperature
findings.mechanism: Positively correlated.
findings.quote: Broadband frontal neural synchronization (higher power) at 4-50 Hz, with a smaller effect at the β-band (13–30 Hz), was observed to be positively correlated with color temperature.

findings.antecedent: Broadband power differences in the frontal regions
findings.consequent: Participants' desired vs. not-desired levels of luminosity
findings.mechanism: Predictive relationship.
findings.quote: Our results indicate that those broadband power differences in the frontal regions are also predictive of participants' desired vs. not-desired levels of luminosity

findings.consequent: Desired vs. not-desired levels of CCT
findings.mechanism: Helped to identify.
findings.quote: and that parietal alpha power helped to identify desired vs not-desired levels of CCT

mechanisms: Modulation of specific EEG band-powers (theta, alpha, beta, gamma) and their ratios (alpha/theta, alpha/beta, alpha/gamma, beta/theta, beta/gamma, gamma/theta) in frontal, central, and parietal brain regions by illuminance and CCT.

Machine learning classification (quadratic kSVM) of EEG data to distinguish between different lighting conditions, subjective mood responses (pleasure, arousal), and behavioral lighting preferences (desired vs. non-desired illumination/CCT).
implementation_implications: Assist architects and engineers in developing lighting plans optimized according to occupants' subjective states (brain activity, lighting adjustment behavior, mood).
Utilize VR simulations for cost-effective testing and optimization of lighting designs.
Potential development of Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) systems for automatic lighting adjustment based on individual user's brain responses.
Improve wellbeing and find applications in treatments like direct light therapy for mood disorders.
Empower disabled individuals with easier interaction with their environment through BCI-controlled lighting.
Combine BCI with VR for fluid interaction testing in virtual environments, applicable to real-world spaces.
Enable evidence-based design approaches for lighting that are more inexpensive and accessible.

tables.description: Top 3 correlations and their linear regression results for both illumination and CCT.

limitations: VR HMD luminance range is limited compared to real-world light sources, diminishing usefulness at very high (blinding effects/glare not accurately reflected) and very low (full scotopic vision range not elicited) illuminance extremes.
Illumination measures (lumens) in VR not validated against standard real-world measurement procedures (lux) and not directly transferable to real-world settings.

Loss of data from 8 participants due to technical problems (excessive EEG motion artifacts, missing/incomplete data, synchronization issues, HMD/EEG battery crashes), resulting in higher-than-expected attrition rate.
Study used a convenience sample composed mostly of undergraduate students at Human Centered Design, Cornell University.

Did not evaluate demographic variables (e.g., age, gender) or other factors (e.g., participant sleep schedules, time of day) that may impact results, potentially affecting machine-learning classification accuracy.
